blocks.text: Line sweep is a beautiful technique for problems about overlapping ranges. Imagine a vertical line sweeping across a timeline from left to right, pausing at every important moment to update a running count.

blocks.alt: Line sweep: convert intervals to events, process left to right, build the answer

blocks.text: It answers questions that plain sorting struggles with, like how many meetings overlap at the busiest minute, or the maximum number of cars on a road at once. It is one of the most satisfying patterns to learn.
The core image is simple: a line moving across time, and a counter that goes up when something starts and down when something ends. The peak of that counter is usually the answer.
Instead of thinking about whole intervals, line sweep breaks each interval into two events: a start and an end. Then it processes all the events in time order.
As the imaginary line sweeps forward, every start event adds one to a running count, and every end event removes one. The count tells you, at any moment, how many intervals are active right there.
The first step is always to turn each interval into two events on the timeline.

codes.python:
intervals = [[1, 4], [2, 5], [7, 9]]
events = []
for start, end in intervals:
    events.append((start, 1))    # a start: add one
    events.append((end, -1))     # an end: remove one
events.sort()                     # process events in time order

blocks.text: Now instead of intervals, you have a sorted list of moments, each carrying a plus one or a minus one. The whole problem becomes a simple walk along this list.
The most common line sweep question is: what is the largest number of intervals overlapping at any single moment? Sweep through the events, keep a running count, and track the highest it reaches.

codes.python:
def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        events.append((start, 1))
        events.append((end, -1))
    events.sort()

    active = 0
    best = 0
    for time, change in events:
        active += change
        best = max(best, active)
    return best

blocks.text: The running count rises and falls as the line sweeps. Its peak is exactly the maximum number of overlapping intervals.
What happens when one interval ends at the exact moment another begins? Do they overlap or not? This tie at the same time is where most line sweep bugs live.

blocks.alt: Tie-breaking at time 5: process END before START to avoid false overlap

blocks.text: If an interval ending at 5 does not clash with one starting at 5, then at time 5 the end should be processed before the start. You arrange the event order to reflect the rule the problem wants.
Decide early whether touching at a point counts as an overlap, then order events at the same time to match. Getting this tie rule right is the whole game in line sweep.
The famous Meeting Rooms II problem asks for the fewest rooms needed so that no meeting is left without a room. This is exactly the maximum overlap question in disguise.
At the busiest moment, however many meetings are happening at once is how many rooms you need. Line sweep gives it to you directly.

codes.python:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    events = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        events.append((start, 1))
        events.append((end, -1))
    # an end at the same time is processed before a start,
    # so a room frees up before the next meeting claims it
    events.sort(key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1]))

    active = best = 0
    for time, change in events:
        active += change
        best = max(best, active)
    return best

blocks.text: Notice the sort puts an end, carrying minus one, before a start, carrying plus one, at the same time. That reuses a room the instant a meeting finishes.
Car Pooling is another line sweep favourite. You pick up and drop off groups of passengers along a road, and you must check you never exceed the car capacity.
Each trip adds passengers at its start point and removes them at its end point. Sweep along the road and check the running total never goes over capacity.
This version uses a fixed timeline array instead of sorted events, which works nicely when the positions are small whole numbers. It is the same plus and minus idea.
The Skyline Problem is the hardest classic in this family. Given the positions and heights of buildings, you must draw the outline they form against the sky.

It is a line sweep too, but with a twist: instead of just counting, at each event you need the current tallest building. That calls for a heap to always know the maximum height as buildings enter and leave.
You do not need to master the skyline yet. Just recognise it as a line sweep where each event updates a running maximum height rather than a simple count.
The My Calendar problems ask you to book events one at a time, rejecting any booking that clashes with an existing one. Each new booking is an overlap check against what is already scheduled.
For a stream of bookings, you keep the existing intervals in an ordered structure so you can quickly find whether a new one overlaps, rather than sweeping everything from scratch each time.
Line sweep comes in two practical flavours, and knowing both helps you pick the right one.
Sorted events
Turn intervals into start and end events, sort them, and walk through. This works for any values, even very large ones, because you only look at the moments that matter.
A timeline array
When the positions are small whole numbers, you can mark plus and minus directly in an array indexed by position, then sweep the array. This is what Car Pooling used, and it is often simpler.
Use sorted events when values can be large or fractional. Use a timeline array when positions are small, bounded whole numbers.

content.title: 10. When to Reach for Line Sweep

blocks.text: Line sweep is the right tool when a problem is about how many things are active at the same time, or where a running total peaks.

items: How many intervals overlap at the busiest moment
The fewest rooms, machines, or resources needed
Whether a running total ever exceeds a limit, like car capacity
Building an outline or profile, such as the skyline

blocks.text: If a problem asks "at most how many at once" or "do we ever exceed", think starts and ends as events, and sweep.
Like most interval work, the cost is dominated by sorting the events.

blocks.text: The timeline array version can be even faster when positions are small, since it skips the sort and simply walks the array once.

items: Getting the tie rule wrong when an end and a start share the same time
Forgetting to sort the events before sweeping
Using a timeline array when the positions are too large to fit
Adding at the start but forgetting to subtract at the end
Tracking the count but forgetting to record its peak value

blocks.text: When a line sweep answer is off by one at the busy moments, the tie rule at equal times is almost always the culprit. Check whether ends should come before starts.
How is line sweep different from just sorting intervals?
Sorting intervals is great for merging and clash checks. Line sweep goes further by counting how many overlap at once, by splitting each interval into a start and an end event.
When should an end come before a start at the same time?
When touching at a point does not count as an overlap. Processing the end first frees the resource before the new one claims it.
Do I always need sorted events?
No. When positions are small whole numbers, a timeline array with plus and minus marks is simpler and can skip the sort entirely.
Why does the skyline problem need a heap?
Because at each event you need the current tallest building, not just a count. A heap keeps the maximum height ready as buildings enter and leave.
These problems build real fluency with the line sweep technique.

items: Meeting Rooms II: find the fewest rooms for a set of meetings.
Car Pooling: check you never exceed the car capacity.
The Skyline Problem: draw the outline of a set of buildings.
My Calendar I: accept bookings only when they do not clash.

blocks.text: Start with Meeting Rooms II, since it is the purest form of the maximum overlap idea. Once that clicks, the others are the same technique with a small twist.
